title: Secrets and API keys
summary: Where API keys may live, why the browser is public, which Supabase key goes where, and what to do in the first hour after a key leaks.
youWillLearn: Why anything in browser code is public, including keys
How environment variables keep secrets out of code, and what NEXT_PUBLIC_ really does
The difference between Supabase's anon key and its service role key
How to rotate a leaked key without breaking the live app

glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.secret: Any value that grants access or spends money: API keys, database passwords, signing keys.
glossary.API key: A long string that tells a paid service like the Claude API which account to charge and trust.
glossary.browser bundle: The JavaScript files every visitor downloads to run your app. Anyone can open and read them.
glossary.environment variable: A named value given to your code by the machine it runs on, so it does not have to be written in the code itself.
glossary.anon key: Supabase's public key for browser code. Safe to publish only because RLS limits what it can read and change. Newer projects call it the publishable key.
glossary.service role key: Supabase's master key that skips RLS. Server only. Newer projects call it the secret key.
glossary.secret scanning: A GitHub feature that looks for known key formats in pushed code and can block the push or alert you.
glossary.rotate: Replace a key with a new one and switch the old one off, ideally without downtime.

steps.title: The Summarize button, first draft
body: Notely, our notes app, gets a Summarize button. It sends a note to the Claude API, Anthropic's AI, which writes a summary.
Claude knows whom to bill by an API key, a long password-like string. This first draft has no app server: Maya's browser, the screen she uses Notely in, holds the key and calls Claude itself.

callout.text: New to Notely? The 4-minute Meet Notely lesson at the start of the Data module shows the whole app, part by part.

scene.caption: The browser holds the key and calls the Claude API itself.

steps.title: A key in the browser is a key for everyone
body: Every visitor downloads Notely's page code, key included. A stranger opens DevTools, the browser's built-in developer tools, copies the key and runs their own AI app on it.
Claude cannot tell the difference. Every call is billed to Notely.

callout.text: Bots scan public sites and code for keys all day. A leaked AI key can run up a large bill before anyone notices. A spend limit at the provider caps the damage.

changes: + Stranger: someone who copied the key from the page
~ Browser: its key is readable by anyone
~ AI bill 3 → 900 $/day

scene.caption: The key ships to every visitor. A stranger calls Claude on Notely's account.

steps.title: Two worlds: public and private
body: Code that runs in the browser is public: it ships to every visitor in the browser bundle. Code on the app server, the computer running Notely's code, is private.
So a secret lives only on the server. The browser asks Notely's server, and the server calls Claude with the key. The stranger's copy still works, for now.

callout.text: A shop keeps the safe key behind the counter. Customers ask the cashier for change. They never get the key.

changes: + App Server: the private side, now holding the key
~ Browser: no key any more

scene.caption: The browser calls Notely's server. Only the server holds the key and talks to Claude.

steps.title: Environment variables keep keys out of code
body: Do not type the key into the code, or it lands in Git, the history of all changes. Put it in an environment variable: a named value the host (here Vercel, which runs the server) hands your code as it starts.
On your laptop: a .env.local file that Git ignores. On Vercel: the project settings. Code only says process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

callout.text: On Cloudflare Workers the same idea is wrangler secret put NAME. Each host has its own settings page, and none of them want keys in the code.

code.code:
# Server only
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=...

# Public on purpose: shipped to the browser
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://xyz.supabase.co
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=...
code.caption: Commit a .env.example with the names and empty values, so teammates know what to set.

changes: + Env Vars: the host's settings, handing the key to the code
~ Stranger and Claude API step back

scene.caption: The key lives in the host's settings. The code only reads it by name.

steps.title: NEXT_PUBLIC_ means "publish this"
body: Notely's code is written with Next.js, a toolkit for web apps. It copies every variable whose name starts with NEXT_PUBLIC_ into the browser bundle. Vite, another toolkit, does the same with VITE_.
So the prefix is a decision to publish. NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY would be this lesson's first mistake, written as a name.

code.caption: This file runs on the server only. The key never leaves it.

changes: + Env Vars → Browser: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values copied in
~ Browser: receives the public values only

scene.caption: Variables with the public prefix get copied into the browser. The rest stay on the server.

steps.title: Supabase's two keys: anon and service role
body: The database, where Notely keeps its notes, has two keys. The anon key is meant for the browser. It is safe to publish only because RLS, last lesson's row rules, limits what it can do.
The service role key skips RLS entirely. It belongs on the server, for admin jobs like a nightly cleanup.

callout.text: Newer Supabase projects name these the publishable key and the secret key. The split is the same: one for browsers behind RLS, one for trusted servers only.

changes: + Database: Notely's notes, with two keys
− Env Vars
~ Browser uses the anon key, App Server the service key

scene.caption: The anon key goes through RLS. The service role key skips it, so it stays on the server.

steps.title: Git never forgets
body: Someone commits the .env.local file, Claude key inside, and deletes it in the next commit. The key is still in the history on GitHub, where Notely's code is stored. Bots scan GitHub for keys constantly.
GitHub's secret scanning catches many known key formats. Still, treat a key that was ever pushed as leaked, even in a private repo.
changes: + GitHub: stores Notely's code and its full history
− Database, and the Browser steps back
~ Stranger: finds the key in the history too
~ App Server: holds the Claude key again

scene.caption: A deleted .env file still sits in the history. Anyone with the repo can find the key.

steps.title: Rotating a leaked key
body: Deleting the file does not help. You rotate: create a new key, put it in the host's settings, redeploy, then switch the old key off at Anthropic. Last, check usage logs for calls you did not make.
If the key is being abused right now, switch it off first and accept a few minutes of downtime.

code.code:
# 1. Create a new key in the provider's console
# 2. Swap it in Vercel
vercel env rm ANTHROPIC_API_KEY production
vercel env add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY production
# 3. Redeploy: env changes only reach new deploys
vercel --prod
# 4. Revoke the old key in the provider's console
code.caption: Then set a spend limit in the provider's console, so the next leak is capped.

changes: + Env Vars: now holding the new key
~ Claude API: the old key is switched off
~ AI bill 900 → 3 $/day

scene.caption: A new key goes into the settings, the app redeploys, and the stranger's copy stops working.

steps.title: A five-minute key audit
body: Before Notely goes live, check three things. Is a key anywhere in the code or the history? Which variables are published to the browser? Is .env.local ignored by Git?
Anthropic keys start with sk-ant-, which makes them easy to search for.

callout.text: Ask Claude Code: does any file marked 'use client' (browser code) import a secret? Does any NEXT_PUBLIC_* variable hold one? Is .env* in .gitignore? Did a real key ever go into a test, seed script or README?

code.code:
git grep -n "sk-ant-"                 # in the code now
git log --all --oneline -S "sk-ant-"  # ever in history
git grep -n "NEXT_PUBLIC_"            # published on purpose?
git check-ignore -v .env.local        # should print a rule

changes: − Stranger
~ GitHub: no live key; the old one in history is dead

scene.caption: Secrets on the server, public values in the browser, no live key in Git.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Browser code is public, so secrets live only on the server, passed in as environment variables. NEXT_PUBLIC_ means published. The Supabase anon key is public by design and leans on RLS; the service role key is for servers.
A key that ever reached Git is leaked: rotate it, redeploy, switch the old one off, check usage.
changes: − GitHub
~ App Server: the only place the key lives

scene.caption: One key, in one place: the server's settings.

quiz.question: Claude Code put NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in .env.local so browser code can call Claude. The file is git-ignored. Is the key safe?

options.why: Git is not the problem here. The prefix tells Next.js to copy the value into the browser bundle, so every visitor gets it.

options.text: No. Move the call to a server route and drop the prefix.
options.why: Only server code should hold the key. The browser calls your route, and your route calls Claude.

options.text: Yes, if the site uses HTTPS.
options.why: HTTPS protects data in transit. The visitor still receives the key and can read it in DevTools.

quiz.question: Which Supabase key is fine to ship in browser code?

options.text: The anon (publishable) key, as long as RLS is on.
options.why: It is designed to be public. RLS policies decide what each user can do with it.

options.text: The service role (secret) key, if the code is minified.
options.why: Minifying does not hide strings. Anyone could read it and skip RLS on every table.

options.text: Neither. The browser must never talk to Supabase.
options.why: Talking to Supabase from the browser is normal and intended, with the anon key and RLS.

quiz.question: Maya notices she pushed a real API key to a private GitHub repo an hour ago. What is the right first move?

options.text: Delete the file in a new commit.
options.why: The key stays in history. Anyone with access to the repo, now or later, can still find it.

options.text: Nothing, because the repo is private.
options.why: Private repos get shared, cloned, forked and connected to tools. Treat any pushed key as leaked.

options.text: Make a new key, deploy it, switch the old one off, then check usage.
options.why: Rotating makes the leaked copy worthless. Checking usage shows whether anyone already used it.

takeaways: Browser code is public. A secret lives only in server code, passed in as an environment variable.
NEXT_PUBLIC_ and VITE_ mean "ship this to every visitor". Never put a secret behind them.
The Supabase anon key is public and relies on RLS. The service role key skips RLS and stays on the server.
A key that was ever pushed to Git is leaked. Rotate: new key, redeploy, switch the old one off, check usage.
Set a spend limit at every paid API provider, so a leak has a ceiling.
